title: Analysis of Sediment Concentration Profiles and Diffusion Processes in Gravity-Flow Water Transport Pipelines for Recognizing Siltation Hazards
content: Gravity-fed pipelines combine a small footprint, low leakage, and energy-efficient conveyance. However, sediment-rich flows promote bottom deposition during low-discharge operation and drawdown, reducing capacity and water-supply reliability. Existing critical non-depositing velocity relationships, largely derived from small pipes or open channels, inadequately explain profiles with a steep near-bottom decline, an intermediate low-gradient plateau, and a second decline. Coupled effects of particle-size distribution, discharge, diameter, and development length also remain unresolved. This study examined gravity-fed Yellow River diversion pipelines on the Loess Plateau China, where the deposition is particularly problematic. Sediment characterization and settling observations after stirring cessation were combined with Eulerian multiphase simulations and analytical settling–diffusion analysis. Twenty-seven cases covered diameters of 0.8, 1.2, and 1.6 m, discharges of 0.2–1.0 m³/s, and inlet mass concentration of 10–30 kg/m³. Outlet profiles showed bottom enrichment and upper-region depletion, with stronger nonuniformity at lower discharge. Larger diameters shortened the plateau and shifted the second decline toward the bottom. The analysis distinguished absolute enrichment, relative enrichment, and profile-shape changes. It also established conditions for inferring deposition and critical non-depositing velocities from concentration distributions. These findings inform low-discharge deposition-risk assessment, sediment-removal thresholds, and operational scheduling.
